intro: The command icon is the looped square symbol printed on the Command key of Apple keyboards. In an interface it signals a keyboard shortcut or a quick action launcher: tap it to open a command palette, show a shortcut cheat sheet or hint that a feature can be triggered from the keyboard.
meaning: The four-looped shape is a Scandinavian place of interest sign, picked for the first Macintosh in 1984 after Steve Jobs felt the Apple logo appeared in menus too often. People now read it as power user territory: shortcuts, palettes and hidden speed. It should not be confused with the Windows Ctrl key, which has no symbol, or with the >_ prompt, which means typing into a terminal.
uses: Productivity app sidebar: opens a command palette where people search for actions instead of hunting through menus.
Menu items in a Mac web app: sits before the shortcut letter, showing that the action has a keyboard equivalent.
Onboarding tooltip: highlights the shortcut that opens quick search, teaching new users a faster route through the product.
Help centre article: marks the section listing every shortcut, grouped by editing, navigation and formatting tasks.
tips: Detect the platform and show Ctrl as text on Windows and Linux, since the looped symbol only matches the physical key on Apple keyboards.
When used inline next to letters, size the glyph to the cap height of the text so the shortcut reads as one unit.
Give an icon-only palette button a label naming the action, and add aria-keyshortcuts so the key combination is announced too.

faq.q: What is the mac command icon called?
faq.a: It is usually called the command symbol, cloverleaf or looped square, and Unicode lists it as the place of interest sign, U+2318. On a Mac it sits on the Command key beside the space bar and appears in menus next to every shortcut that uses that key.

faq.q: Is the cmd icon the same as a keyboard shortcut icon?
faq.a: Not quite: the looped symbol stands for one specific Apple modifier key, while a general shortcut symbol usually shows a keyboard or keycap to mean shortcuts in any app. Use the command symbol for Mac shortcut hints and a keyboard glyph for a cross-platform shortcut list.
